boundary_spanning_measures.report_type_note: Expatriate and local humanitarian aid workers rated their field office manager.
boundary_spanning_measures.source_quote: We measured boundary-spanning leadership using a three-item scale adopted from the Intergroup Rhetoric Scale by Rast (2013). We separately asked expatriate and local respondents to describe whether their field office manager (1) “interacts frequently with both local and expatriate employees”, (2) “is equally available for the local and expatriate employees during office hours”, and (3) “puts a lot of effort in strengthening the relationship between the local and expatriate group”. Participants completed this measure via a 7-point Likert scale (1 = not at all, 7 = very much), with high scores indicating stronger perceptions that the field office manager engages in boundary spanning. Factor loadings for each item were .83, .83, and .79, respectively, with a Cronbach's alpha of .86.

non_bs_measures.source_quote: We then measured the perceived effectiveness of collaboration using a three-item scale adopted from Jap (2001). Participants completed this measure via a 7-point Likert scale (1 = strongly disagree, 7 = strongly agree), with high scores indicating a high degree of perceived collaboration between groups. Factor loadings for each item were .84, .82, and .95, respectively, with a Cronbach's alpha of .90.

To measure leader in-group prototypicality, we utilized a three-item scale adopted from van Knippenberg and van Knippenberg (2005). Participants completed the measure via a 7-point Likert scale (1 = not at all, 7 = very much), with high scores indicating stronger perceptions that the field office manager is highly in-group prototypical for the respondent's group. Factor loadings for each item were .76, .89, and .88, respectively, with a Cronbach's alpha of .88.

We developed an item for field learning based on reports from the field-level learning and organizational learning literatures (e.g., Ahmad & Schroeder, 2003; Fugate, Stank, & Mentzer, 2009). Namely, we asked: (1) “In comparison to other comparable field offices, how would you judge the operational learning of your field office (i.e., learning between programs, expatriates, and local employees)?” Participants completed both items via a 7‐point Likert scale ranging from −3 = far worse (1) to +3 = far better (7), with high scores suggesting a high level of perceived learning or creativity.

Likewise, we used the team creativity literature and humanitarian case studies (e.g., Hargadon & Bechky, 2006; Ramalingam et al., 2009) to construct a single-item scale for field creativity. We asked: (1) “In comparison to other comparable field offices, how would you judge the operational creativity of your field office (i.e., finding solutions to difficult problems)?” Participants completed both items via a 7‐point Likert scale ranging from −3 = far worse (1) to +3 = far better (7), with high scores suggesting a high level of perceived learning or creativity.
